target_customer: Consumers, mostly Gen Z friend groups, using free group video chat with screen sharing
problem: Friends wanted to share what they were doing on their phone while video chatting, and group video apps did not let them share any app.
business_model: Free consumer app, no revenue model found
product_category: Social group video chat with screen sharing

founders.name: Ethan Sutin
previous_startups: Bee (YC page says acquired by Amazon)
founders.background_notes: From the YC page; no education or employers listed.

founders.name: Esther Crawford
founders.background_notes: Named as co-founder and CEO in the seed announcement coverage and the DocSend profile; not listed on the YC page.

technical_complexity.rationale: Real-time group video plus phone screen capture on iOS and Android is standard with managed video APIs, with some hard parts in low latency screen sharing on mobile.

defensibility.rationale: Features could be copied by larger video apps; only friend group habit offered lock-in.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Twitter acquired the team in December 2020 and shut the app down on 12 December 2020, folding the idea into its own conversations products.

market_need_then: Group video among friends and screen sharing were already popular, and the pandemic in 2020 boosted demand per press coverage, but no dated 2018 demand source was opened.

branding.domain_note: Used squadapp.io, not an exact .com; the site returned an error on fetch.

identity.voice_and_tone: Gen Z social hangout framing in press coverage

branding.community_and_virality: Press coverage on TechCrunch of the desktop launch in 2020 and a Gen Z hangout angle; no evidence of merch or fan accounts.

brand_strength.rationale: A short, friendly, generic word with decent tech press coverage and a CEO who was visible on social media, but no sources on the brand itself.

pivots.why: A search summary of a DocSend profile says the company pivoted from Molly to Squad in August 2018; the reason was not read.

outcome_analysis: Squad built a mobile and then desktop group video app with screen sharing, raised a 5 million dollar seed in August 2019 led by First Round, and was bought by Twitter in December 2020 for undisclosed terms. The app shut down the next day while the team joined Twitter, and the CEO said she chose the sale over raising a Series A, so it reads as a team acquisition rather than a scaled product exit.
notes: The pre-pivot company Molly raised about 2.2 million dollars and 500 thousand dollars on SAFEs in April 2018 per one search summary of DocSend; unverified and not recorded as rounds. Search summaries also gave 7.2 million dollars total raised. Squad's site did not load, so only press was used for the product. Competition search returned only 2020 coverage, so no dated competitor near the 2018 batch is listed. Houseparty is a likely rival but had no 2018 source.
